# Fix perspective

- Route: `/tools/fix-perspective-photo`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `fix-perspective-photo`

## Summary

Drag four corners to correct keystone and converging verticals, then auto-crop the result. (Photo editing)

## Details

Perspective correction in the Aperture Geometry panel is a four-corner projective transform. Press Drag the corners and pull each corner of the frame outward or inward; the editor builds the homography that maps the unit square onto your quadrilateral (Heckbert's construction) and inverse-maps every output pixel through it, sampling the source bilinearly. Because it is a true projective map rather than a stretch, the converging verticals of a building shot from the street become parallel while straight lines stay straight. Perspective, rotation, flips and crop are all applied in one resample before any adjustment layer. With Auto-crop to the largest rectangle on, the frame is trimmed to the biggest clean rectangle of the original aspect; off, the stretched corners are filled with transparency, the edge or a color.
### What it does
- Maps the frame through a projective transform defined by four corner offsets, each clamped to half the frame so a corner can never cross the middle.
- Corrects keystone in either axis: pull the top corners outward to fix verticals that converge upward, or the side corners to square a document photographed at an angle.
- Resamples once, bilinearly, from the original pixels for crop, perspective, flip and rotate together, so the corrected image is not softened by repeated passes.
- Auto-crops to the largest centered rectangle whose whole perimeter samples real pixels, or keeps the full canvas with your chosen fill.
- Exports the corrected original at full resolution on our server with the same homography coefficients the preview used.
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: The Geometry panel opens with the Perspective section; press Drag the corners.
2. Pull the corners: For a building that leans back, drag the top-left corner left and the top-right corner right until the verticals read as parallel. Drag a few percent at a time.
3. Decide the crop: Auto-crop trims to the largest rectangle. Switch it off and choose Transparent, Stretch the edge or Color to keep the whole canvas.
4. Export: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF, rendered from the original. Reset perspective at any time to return to zero offsets.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Transparent corner fill needs PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF; a JPG export shows the fill as black.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- Each corner stores an offset (x, y) in units of the post-rotation canvas size, so tl = (-0.06, 0) means the top-left corner is moved outward by 6 percent of the width. The four target points, tl, tr = (1 + x, y), br = (1 + x, 1 + y) and bl = (x, 1 + y), define a quadrilateral, and the unit square is mapped onto it with the eight-coefficient homography x = (a u + b v + c) / (g u + h v + 1), y = (d u + e v + f) / (g u + h v + 1), computed with Heckbert's closed form; a parallelogram (zero projective terms) reduces to the affine case.
- For a 4000 x 6000 portrait with tl.x = -0.06 and tr.x = +0.06, the coefficients are a = 1.12, b = 0.06, c = -0.06, e = 1.12 and h = 0.12 with the rest 0: the top row of the output samples a source row 12 percent wider than itself, so verticals that converged by 12 percent of the frame width become parallel.
- Every output pixel center is sent through the homography, then the flips and the inverse rotation, to a continuous source coordinate and bilinearly interpolated from its four neighbors; samples outside the source take the fill, and the alpha channel is interpolated the same way so a transparent fill has a soft one-pixel border.
- Auto-crop runs a 30-step binary search for the largest centered rectangle of the canvas aspect whose 100 perimeter samples all land inside the source. For the 6 percent correction above it keeps 89.83 percent of each side, 3593 x 5390 pixels, 80.7 percent of the 24 MP original; a 10 percent correction keeps 71.6 percent. Pulling the corners inward instead needs no crop at all because every output pixel maps inside the source.
- The Aperture preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy, the export is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance; for geometry that is a maximum of 2 8-bit levels in the interior with a 2 px border excluded, while color operations are held to a mean of 1 level and grain is exact.
### When not to use it
Do not reach for the perspective tool when a line is curved rather than converging: barrel distortion from a wide lens needs a radial correction that this editor does not offer, and a projective map will leave the curve in place. A simple tilt is a rotation and belongs to Straighten, which costs fewer pixels. Very large corrections, above roughly 15 percent of the frame, stretch the far edge so much that detail turns soft and the crop removes a third of the picture; reshoot from farther back with a longer focal length when you can.
### Use cases
- Architecture shot from the street: Pull the top corners outward 4 to 8 percent until the window columns are parallel; expect to keep 80 to 90 percent of the pixels.
- Whiteboards and posters: Drag each corner of the frame onto the corner of the board; turn auto-crop off and crop manually to the board afterward.
- Interiors with a wide lens: Small corrections of 2 to 3 percent on the top corners square up door frames without the stretched look of a large fix.
- Product packshots: Square up a box photographed slightly from above so its front face is a true rectangle before cutting out the background.
### FAQ
Q: How far can I drag a corner?
A: Each corner offset is clamped to plus or minus half the canvas size in each axis, so a corner can approach the middle of the frame but never cross it. Corrections beyond about 15 percent usually look stretched anyway.
Q: Why does the auto-crop remove so much when I fix a tall building?
A: Pulling the top corners outward means the top of the output has to sample a wider strip of the source than exists, so the sides must be trimmed until the whole perimeter is real pixels. A 6 percent pull on a 3:2 portrait keeps about 81 percent of the pixels.
Q: Can I combine perspective with straightening?
A: Yes. Rotation is applied first, then the perspective offsets are interpreted on the rotated canvas, and both go through one bilinear resample, so draw the horizon line first and then square the verticals.
Q: Is this the same as lens distortion correction?
A: No. Barrel and pincushion distortion bend straight lines and need a radial model. The perspective tool only handles converging lines; a bent line stays bent after it.
Q: What does Reset perspective do?
A: It sets all four corner offsets back to zero and removes the homography, leaving any rotation, flip and crop you set in place. The button is disabled while the offsets are already zero.
Q: Will the corrected photo be blurry?
A: Stretched regions are interpolated and lose a little sharpness, roughly in proportion to the stretch; a 6 percent correction is barely detectable at 100 percent zoom. A light Sharpen layer above it restores the edge contrast.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when vertical lines converge, as with a building shot from below, or a document was photographed at an angle, and someone wants it squared by dragging four corners, then auto-cropped.
When to send them elsewhere: A simple tilt belongs in Straighten a photo (straighten-photo). Curved lines from a wide-angle lens are not corrected. To get a clean flat scan of a paper document use AI Document Scan (ai-document-scan).
Related tools: straighten-photo (simple tilt correction); ai-document-scan (scan a photographed document); crop-image (custom crop afterwards); sharpen-photo-online (recover detail after correcting)
